title: Lithography
summary: Printing with light: resolution, EUV scanners, High-NA and the photon budget.

links.why: one step of the patterning loop

ideas.how: lines finer than the light can draw forced the move to EUV

measures.how: each smaller node needs finer printing

challenges.title: Print the finest lines
challenges.task: Find the smallest pitch each scanner can still print.

learn.plain: Lithography is printing with light through a stencil that is shrunk four times. When lines get thinner than the light can draw, engineers switch to shorter light (EUV), bigger lenses, cleverly angled lighting, or split the pattern across two stencils.
learn.engineer: Half-pitch resolution is k₁λ/NA, with practical single-exposure k₁ down to about 0.25 using off-axis illumination; depth of focus scales as λ/NA², so High-NA trades focus margin for resolution. High-NA uses anamorphic 4×/8× reduction, which halves the exposure field to 26 × 16.5 mm. EUV stochastics (photon shot noise, secondary electrons, resist chemistry) push dose up and set line-edge roughness and missing-contact rates.

quiz.q: In the Rayleigh equation, which change lets you print smaller features?
options: A shorter wavelength or a larger numerical aperture
quiz.why: Half-pitch = k₁ · λ / NA, so shrinking λ or raising NA (or lowering k₁) prints finer lines.

quiz.q: Why does an EUV scanner use mirrors instead of lenses?
options: EUV light is absorbed by glass and even air
quiz.why: So the light path is in vacuum and every optic is a multilayer mirror that reflects about 70%.

quiz.q: Why can a low EUV dose cause defects?
options: Too few photons hit each spot, so random counts make rough or missing features
quiz.why: This is the stochastics problem, a key trade-off against throughput.
